The Standard & Poor's 500 index rose 1.1% this week as hyperscalers showed the mega spend on the artificial intelligence buildout is being monetized.

The market benchmark ended the week at 7,489.72. The index is now down 0.1% quarter-to-date but up 9.4% year-to-date.

Microsoft (MSFT) and Amazon.com (AMZN) rose this week as quarterly results from the tech giants showed revenue growth in areas related to AI products and services, helping calm worries surrounding hundreds of billions of dollars of investments earmarked for the AI buildout.

Microsoft reported triple-digit AI annual recurring revenue growth and an accelerating Azure trajectory into the end of 2026, Dan Ives, global head of technology at Wedbush Securities, said in a note to clients. The software behemoth's quarterly results, which included Azure's full-year revenue surpassing $100 billion for the first time, reinforced the idea that "any knee-jerk reactions to the elevated capex framework represent strong buying opportunities," Ives said.

Shares of Microsoft were up 22% this week.

The consumer discretionary sector in the S&P 500 had the largest percentage gain of the week, up 8.3%, followed by a 5.4% advance in communication services and a 1.2% rise in consumer staples.

Sales at Amazon's cloud computing unit delivered the fastest growth in 18 quarters, helping the e-commerce giant exceed market expectations for Q2 earnings and revenue. Shares jumped 17% this week even as the e-commerce behemoth expanded its capital expenditure by about $20 billion to $220 billion.

A consortium of banks led by Morgan Stanley (MS) is in talks to lend $15 billion to a data-center developer to build a campus and power plant for Anthropic in Texas, The Wall Street Journal reported Thursday, citing people familiar with the matter. Alphabet's (GOOG, GOOGL) Google would provide financial guarantees and chips for the project. Shares of Alphabet are up 12% this week.

The three worst-performing S&P 500 sectors this week were utilities, real estate and materials, down 4.2%, 2.2%, and 1.7%, respectively.

C.H. Robinson Worldwide (CHRW) said a jury in Texas issued a $604 million advisory verdict against the firm and two other defendants in a lawsuit stemming from a trucking accident involving an independent motor carrier. Shares declined 21% this week.

title: Marvell Technology Is Betting More Of Its Revenue On One End Market
detail:
Marvell Technology Is Betting More Of Its Revenue On One End Market
Trefis Team
Fri, July 31, 2026 at 10:09 AM PDT 4 min read
MRVL
INTC
NVDA
QCOM
AVGO
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Image from Pixabay

Three-quarters of its sales already come from data centers, and the company's own guidance widens that share even as it plans for cloud spending growth to cool.

Marvell Technology (MRVL) now draws roughly three-quarters of its sales from a single end market. In fiscal Q1 2027, the most recent quarter reported, the data center end market accounted for 76% of what the company sold, up from 74% in fiscal Q4 2026. On $8.7 billion of revenue over the trailing twelve months and a market value of about $162 billion, that share is the number a holder should be able to name. Not the growth rate, and not the margin: how much of the business answers to a single category of buyer.

Why The Guidance Pushes That 76% Higher

One quarter's step from 74% to 76% proves nothing by itself. The guidance does. Management guides data center sales up about 50% in fiscal 2027, then about 55% in fiscal 2028, after a 46% increase in fiscal 2026. Nothing else in the company comes close to that pace: communications and other end markets, which produced $585 million of revenue in fiscal Q1 2027, are expected to grow about 10% in fiscal 2027 and at a low single-digit rate in fiscal 2028. If those figures land as given, the part of the business that could dilute the concentration is the part growing slowest, which makes 76% a floor for the mix rather than a high-water mark.

A Three-Quarter Share Set By A Handful Of Cloud Budgets

What makes a mix like that uncomfortable is who decides it. Management's own account of where the spending lands is blunt: the top four U.S. hyperscalers spend the bulk of the capital budgets, so that is where the dollars go. On that telling, the largest buyers behind that 76% are a short list. And management is planning for cloud capital spending growth to moderate to around the 30% range in fiscal 2028 while planning for its own data center revenue to accelerate to about 55%, on the stated expectation that its interconnect business keeps outpacing that spending. The load-bearing assumption is therefore not that the build-out continues. It is that Marvell keeps taking a bigger share of spending that is growing more slowly than it did.

Does 18.5 Times Sales Leave Any Cushion?

All of this would matter less at a modest price. The stock trades around $183, about 58% of its 52-week high of $316.35, though it is still up about 140% over the trailing twelve months against 17.7% for the S&P 500. Even down that far from the high, it changes hands at 18.5 times sales, against a ten-year range running from 3.0 to 30.1. A price-to-sales multiple in the top decile of its own decade suggests the market is already paying for the guided ramp rather than waiting to see it, which is what turns a question about mix into a question about price. The underlying improvement is real: an operating margin of 16.4% over the trailing twelve months against a three-year average of 0.2%.

title: Nvidia’s Valuation Gap With AMD Just Got Bigger
detail:
Nvidia’s Valuation Gap With AMD Just Got Bigger
Insider Monkey Team
Fri, July 31, 2026 at 9:51 AM PDT 3 min read
NVDA
AMD
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) dropped nearly 4% on July 29, its third sharp pullback in a week, and now trades well off its 52 week high. That sounds bad, but the sell off has pushed Nvidia's valuation to its lowest since 2019, even as the company posted a record quarter. The gap between a cheaper stock and a business still growing fast is what makes Nvidia worth a close look right now.

A Business Still Firing on All Cylinders

Nvidia's most recent quarter (FQ1 2027) delivered $81.6 billion in revenue, a record and an 85% jump from a year earlier. The company already has roughly $1 trillion in confirmed orders for its Blackwell and Vera Rubin chips through 2027, and it expects hyperscaler AI spending to keep climbing toward $3 trillion to $4 trillion a year by decade's end.

Nvidia is also branching out. Its new Vera server CPU targets a $200 billion market, with $20 billion in Vera revenue expected this fiscal year alone despite only recently shipping as a standalone product. On the inference side, its deal with Groq in late 2025 added language processing units built for the decoding stage of AI inference, broadening Nvidia beyond training chips.

Is TSM a good stock to buy?
How Nvidia Stacks Up Against AMD

Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD) competes directly with Nvidia for the same hyperscaler buildout in both GPUs and data center CPUs. Nvidia trades at roughly 22 times forward earnings versus about 67 times for AMD, making it by far the cheaper of the two assuming that NVDA's earnings are sustainable in the long-term. Hedge funds have been adding to both: Nvidia was held by 275 funds in the first quarter of 2026, up from 264, while AMD was held by 134, up from 132. Short sellers are more skeptical of AMD, with 2.45% of its float sold short against 1.39% for Nvidia.

Where the Bull Case Gets Shaky

The most persistent worry is Nvidia's own customers. Hyperscalers are building custom AI chips in house to cut their reliance on Nvidia's GPUs, a long-term risk even while today's demand stays strong. Wall Street already expects a slowdown, with consensus estimates calling for 219% cumulative revenue growth from fiscal 2026 through fiscal 2029, well below the 700% Nvidia posted over the prior three years.

The bigger flashpoint this month is financing. Nvidia is reportedly in talks to guarantee as much as $250 billion in data center lease payments so OpenAI can use a SoftBank facility, on top of up to $350 billion in GPU purchase financing for OpenAI. Combined with a new arrangement worth more than $500 billion with SK Group, the deals have revived worries about circular financing, in which a chipmaker helps fund the very companies buying its products. Nvidia shares fell nearly 5% on the initial reports.

Image from Pixabay

Just over half of revenue still leans on a shrinking handset market, and the businesses meant to replace it do not reach their targeted scale for years.

How Far Has The Market Already Marked This Stock Down?

At $151, the stock has given back 6.9% across its last two sessions, leaving it at about 58% of its 52-week high of $259.9 and below both its 50-day average of $199.28 and its 200-day average of $167.93. Over the past year, it is down 4.5% while the S&P 500 returned 17.7%. The market is not ignoring the risk. The harder question, if you own it, is whether it is in the price or only starting to arrive.

How Much Of The Company Still Rides On Handsets?

Just over half. Qualcomm (QCOM) reported $9.9 billion of revenue in fiscal Q3 2026, and $5.1 billion came from handset chips inside QCT, a number management ties to industry-wide memory dynamics squeezing the smartphone market. The slowdown behind it is not fresh. Revenue over the trailing twelve months is $44.1 billion, up 1.9% year over year against a 15.8% pace a year earlier, and the quarterly year-over-year rate has run 10.0%, then 5.0%, then -3.5%, and -4.0% in the most recent quarter.

Why Is The Revenue Guide Rising While The Earnings Guide Falls?

Because the cost of building the chips is climbing faster than the selling price. Management's fiscal Q4 2026 guidance puts revenue at $9.7 billion to $10.5 billion, above the $9.6 billion guided for fiscal Q3, and non-GAAP earnings per share at $2.05 to $2.25, a range whose midpoint sits below both the $2.20 guided for that quarter and the $2.21 actually delivered. By its own account, the industry is absorbing a broad-based increase in input costs across wafer fabrication, assembly, test, advanced packaging and memory, and QCT gross margins will sit slightly below their historical range; the baseline business normally runs a 48% to 50% gross margin. Price increases in the double digits are meant to start closing that gap over the next couple of quarters.

What Could Push The Recovery Further Out?

Two things, both from the company's own disclosures. The first is Apple: management now expects the step-down in Apple product revenue to accelerate from fiscal Q4 2026, with its share of the upcoming iPhone launch materially below the 20% previously estimated, and Apple product revenue falling roughly 50% from that September quarter to the December quarter that follows. The second is that the replacement business arrives at a thinner margin: early data center revenue comes from custom chip work, an effect management sizes at a drag of 1.5% to 2% on QCT's weighted average gross margin. Management targets $40 billion of non-handset revenue by fiscal 2029, with data center revenue forecast to build from $5 billion in fiscal 2027 to $15 billion in fiscal 2029. That would reshape a company that turned over $44.1 billion in the past twelve months, and it is years out.

Photo by deeznutz1 on Pixabay

Intel swung from an operating loss to an operating profit with the costly part of its turnaround still running, and that swing is what the spending debate keeps drowning out.

Intel (INTC) trades at $91.13, about 35% below the $140.94 high it set over the trailing 52 weeks, and it has given back 3.8% over the past three months even after climbing more than fourfold over the past year. Some of that was sector-wide: in one late-July trading session, the shares were down about 6% intraday and AMD roughly 8%, in a wider selloff across semiconductor shares. The rest is an argument about spending: the company raised its 2026 capital budget to more than $20 billion against trailing twelve-month revenue of $57.0 billion. What that argument leaves out is the operating margin: 7.6% over the trailing twelve months, against -8.3% in the same window a year earlier.

How Did A Loss-Making Business Get To A 7.6% Operating Margin?

The path is not a straight line. Operating margin ran -4.4% three years ago, then -8.3% a year ago, then 7.6% over the trailing twelve months, so it got worse before it turned. On trailing twelve-month revenue of $57.0 billion, that is roughly $4.3 billion of operating profit against a loss a year earlier. The turn did not come from gross margin: non-GAAP gross margin held at 42% in fiscal Q2 2026, with fiscal Q3 2026 guidance near 42%. What moved was the top line: year-over-year quarterly revenue growth ran 2.8%, then -4.1%, then 7.2%, and 25% in the most recent quarter.

Which Businesses Are Carrying The Foundry's $2.1 Billion Loss?

Fiscal Q2 2026 shows where the profit sits. The data center and AI group turned $6.3 billion of revenue, up 59% year over year, into $2.5 billion of operating profit, a 40% segment margin, and the PC and edge business turned $8.9 billion into $2.3 billion, or 26%. Intel Foundry lost $2.1 billion in the same quarter, $348 million less than in fiscal Q1 2026, which management credits to better yields, cycle times, and factory scale. A consolidated operating margin already nets the foundry's losses against the product profits, so the trailing twelve-month 7.6% is what is left after the foundry drag, not before it.

Doesn't The 18A Ramp Pull That Margin Straight Back Down?

That is the bear case, and the answer is a qualified yes. Management says the new products becoming a significant part of its mix still sit below the corporate average gross margin because they are early in their life cycle, and in the core PC client segment, 18A is now in volume production across multiple commercial and consumer products. It expects PC consumption down a low double-digit percentage across all of 2026, and calls the shortages in leading-edge wafers, memory and substrates among the most severe in the industry's history. None of that is resolved. Against it sits a cost curve moving the other way: management says it has cut the cost of its main Panther Lake part by roughly 50% so far in 2026, with another 20% on track and more planned for 2027.
